titre: The First Programmable Electronic Computer Stayed Secret for 30 Years
accroche: Textbooks long presented the American ENIAC, in 1945, as the first programmable electronic computer. A British one already existed, classified.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1946, the U.S. Army publicly unveils ENIAC, an electronic calculator with 17,468 vacuum tubes, ever since presented as the first programmable electronic computer in history. The press around the world covers the event. The title, however, had already been taken, by a machine whose existence no one outside a very small circle was allowed to know.

## A machine built for a far tougher cipher than Enigma

At Bletchley Park, telecommunications engineer Tommy Flowers designs and builds Colossus in eleven months, at the Post Office Research Station at Dollis Hill, building on the work of mathematician Max Newman. The machine passes its first tests successfully on December 8, 1943, then breaks its first real message on February 5, 1944, nearly two years before ENIAC.

Colossus did not attack Enigma. Its target was the Lorenz cipher, a twelve-wheel machine far more complex than Enigma's three or four, used for communications between Berlin and army commanders in the field, the Reich's highest level of encryption, whereas Enigma served more tactical and more numerous communications. Breaking Lorenz gave access, in the very words of the Bletchley Park Trust, to an unprecedented level of detail about the German defenses, and a direct glimpse into the thinking of the highest commanders, Hitler included.

## Ten machines, eight destroyed, a secret kept for thirty years

At the end of the war in Europe, ten Colossus machines are operating at Bletchley Park. Eight are destroyed on the orders of the British government, their parts broken to pieces so that no reconstruction would be possible; the last two follow a few years later. The secret is lifted only in stages: from first information made public in 1975, thanks to the research of historian Brian Randell, to a complete 500-page technical report on the Lorenz cipher, published by GCHQ in October 2000, nearly sixty years after the events.

## What the silence did to the history we tell

Colossus thus precedes ENIAC by nearly two years as a programmable electronic computer. But ENIAC got a press conference in 1946; Colossus remained a state secret while the histories of technology were being written without it. It is not the oldest machine that ended up in the textbook's slot. It is the one that could be talked about first. The episode says nothing against ENIAC, a very real and considerable machine; it says something about how a history of technology is built, less from what was done first than from what we were allowed to know first.

repere.texte: Colossus broke its first real message on February 5, 1944, nearly two years before the United States publicly unveiled ENIAC in February 1946. Ten Colossus machines operated at Bletchley Park; eight were destroyed after the war, and the secret was lifted only in stages, from 1975 to 2000.

carte.punch: The real first programmable electronic computer stayed secret for thirty years.
carte.idee: In 1944, the Colossus machine was already breaking the Lorenz cipher at Bletchley Park, two years before ENIAC, long presented as the first programmable electronic computer. Colossus remained a state secret, revealed only in stages, from 1975 to 2000.

quiz.question: Why was the American ENIAC, rather than Colossus, long presented as the first programmable electronic computer?
choix: Because Colossus remained a state secret for decades, whereas ENIAC was publicly unveiled as early as 1946
Because Colossus was not truly programmable, unlike ENIAC
Because Colossus was built after ENIAC, despite a widespread legend to the contrary
Because neither machine was operating before the end of the war
quiz.explication: Colossus broke its first real message as early as February 1944, nearly two years before ENIAC, but it remained a British military secret, whose existence was revealed only in stages, from 1975 to 2000. ENIAC, for its part, got a public announcement as early as 1946, which earned it the “first” spot in collective memory.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which German cipher machine did Colossus attack?
choix: Enigma, in the four-wheel version used by the navy
The twelve-wheel Lorenz cipher, reserved for the high command
The code used by Japanese submarines in the Pacific
Enigma and Lorenz alternately, depending on the urgency of the messages
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Colossus did not attack Enigma. Its target was the Lorenz cipher, a twelve-wheel machine used between Berlin and army commanders, the Reich's highest level of encryption, whereas Enigma served more tactical communications.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happened to the ten Colossus machines after the war?
choix: They were transferred to the University of Manchester
They were preserved intact and put back into service at GCHQ
Eight were destroyed, their parts broken to pieces
Two were sold to the United States, the rest dismantled
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Eight of the ten machines were destroyed on the orders of the British government, their parts broken to pieces so that no reconstruction would be possible. The last two followed a few years later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the secrecy around Colossus finally lifted?
choix: In stages, from first information in 1975 to a report in 2000
All at once, when a thirty-year legal deadline expired
Through the publication of Tommy Flowers's memoirs as early as 1946
It never was, with most of the file remaining classified
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first information was made public in 1975, thanks to the research of historian Brian Randell. It was not until October 2000 that GCHQ published a complete five-hundred-page technical report on the Lorenz cipher.
